meanings.note: Someone who started earlier than you.

examples.trans: school senior
My senior bought me a meal.

meanings.note: Demonstrative pronoun for something near the speaker; often contracted to 이거 in speech.

examples.trans: Did you film this too?
How much is this?
Please give me some water.
Please wait just a moment.

meanings.note: Contraction of 조금

meanings.en: to hold, to carry in one's hand
meanings.note: ㄹ-irregular verb; 들고 가다 means 'to carry along'.

examples.trans: Please take your bag with you.
If it's heavy, I'll carry it.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 홍삼가루 물에 탄 건데 어제 많이 취하셨던 것 같아서요.
examples.trans: I mixed red-ginseng powder in water because it looked like you got really drunk last night.
Here the word for 'red-ginseng powder' is key.

examples.text: 이 스프레이로 물 뿌리고 신디가 깨면 까나리카노를 내밀면 돼.
examples.trans: Spray water with this bottle, and when Cindy wakes up, hand her this fish-sauce coffee.
The topic of water came up during this shoot.

meanings.note: intransitive verb; also means 'to ride' in another sense

examples.text: 불을 줄이지 않으면 고기가 다 타요.
examples.trans: If you don't lower the heat, the meat will burn completely.
Firewood is burning brightly in the stove.

meanings.note: Bound noun often contracted to 거 in everyday speech.

examples.trans: This is my bag.
Because I think I'm late.
Did you hear about this yesterday?
I was busy today because of yesterday.

meanings.en: a lot, much, in large quantity
meanings.note: Adverbial form of 많다 (to be many/much)

examples.trans: I did a lot of work today.
Please eat plenty and enjoy.
Let's got drunk and together today.
I worked hard to got drunk and yesterday too.

meanings.note: Used in -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다 to express 'it seems that...' or 'I think...'.

meanings.en: to be the same, to be like
meanings.note: Compares two things with -와/과 같다.

examples.trans: I think I'm late.
It looks like it's going to rain.

meanings.note: Expresses sudden realization, surprise, or hesitation.

examples.trans: Ah, yes.
Oh, I see!

맞다.gloss: to be right, to be correct

meanings.note: Used to confirm facts or answers.

meanings.en: to fit, to suit, to match
meanings.note: E.g., 사이즈가 맞다 ('the size fits').

examples.trans: Yes, that's my phone number.
These shoes fit my feet perfectly.

meanings.note: Plain first-person singular pronoun used with friends, younger people, or subordinates; contracts to 난 with -는 and becomes 내가 before -가.

examples.trans: I'm going to stay home today.
I'll go first.

examples.text: 그냥 내버려 둬, 쟤 완전 취했어.
examples.trans: Just leave him alone, he is completely wasted.
That's right, Cindy turned out to be a total fan of good looks.

meanings.note: colloquial contraction of 무엇; also used rhetorically to brush off a question

examples.trans: What are you doing now?
Why are you even asking something like that?

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (verb).

examples.text: 너 그만 마셔, 너 그러다 실수할라!
examples.trans: Stop drinking now—keep going like that and you will slip up!
This expression comes from 'you might make a mistake!'.

없다.gloss: to not exist, to not have

meanings.en: to not exist, to not be present

examples.trans: I don't have time right now.
The tickets are all sold out, so there aren't any.
I understand well (specially).
Today is a (specially) busy day.

meanings.note: Used to emphasize an adjective or verb.

examples.trans: It's really pretty.
I'm truly sorry.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 취해서 거짓말을 좀 했는데 준모 선배님이 기억을 하나 못하나 알아내야 한다는 말씀이시죠?
examples.trans: So you told some lies while drunk, and I must find out whether Senior Joon-mo remembers them or not, right?
Here the word for 'memory' is key.

meanings.note: Short-form negation placed directly before verbs and adjectives

examples.trans: I'm not going to the office today.
I haven't watched that movie yet.

meanings.en: to arise, to come up, to occur
meanings.note: Used with feelings, thoughts, or events (e.g. 실감이 나다, 생각이 나다).

examples.trans: A good idea came to mind.
Tears suddenly came to my eyes.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.trans: Do you really not remember anything from the street tent?
Here the word for 'at the street snack tent?' is key.

meanings.note: Interrogative or indefinite pronoun; often shortened to 뭐 in casual speech.

examples.trans: What is your favorite food?
What can I help you with?

meanings.note: Everyday verb for eating a meal or food; honorific equivalent is 드시다.

examples.trans: Let's eat lunch together.
Did you eat breakfast?

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (num).

examples.text: 안 난다니까, 포장마차에서 뭘 먹었길래 7만 원이 나오냐?
examples.trans: I told you I do not remember—what on earth did we eat at a street tent to rack up seventy thousand won?
Here the word for 'seventy thousand' is key.

meanings.note: Bound noun used with Sino-Korean numbers to state prices in South Korean won.

examples.trans: I only have a thousand won.
That is ten thousand won in total.

meanings.en: to appear, be published, be achieved (a score/result)
meanings.note: Used for ratings, test scores, or results coming out

examples.trans: I came outside from the house.
The exam results came out well.
Did you hear about this corporate card?
I was busy today because of corporate card.

meanings.en: to get nicked, dented, or chipped
meanings.note: Passive form of 찍다 ('to strike/poke/stamp').
Used in 사진이 찍히다.

examples.trans: The car got a tiny nick.
The photo came out well.

보다.gloss: to see, to watch; to take (an exam)

meanings.en: to see, to look at, to watch
meanings.note: Primary meaning.
Idiomatic in 시험을 보다.

examples.trans: I watched a movie on the weekend.
I took the driver's license exam.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.trans: Last night you had soju with live octopus and spicy cartilage.
Here the word for 'with soju' is key.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.trans: You are the one who ordered the live octopus!
Here the word for 'live octopus!' is key.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.trans: Last night you had soju with live octopus and spicy cartilage.
Here the word for 'spicy pork cartilage' is key.

meanings.note: Auxiliary adjective attached to a verb stem with -고 (-고 싶다).

examples.trans: I want to go to Korea.
I want to drink a cup of coffee.

meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 예진이가 먹고 싶은 거 위주로 시켰구먼, 걔가 산낙지 킬러거든.
examples.trans: Ye-jin clearly ordered all her own favorites—she is crazy about live octopus.
Here the word for 'mainly around' is key.

meanings.en: to make someone do, to assign work
meanings.note: Causative verb; e.g., 일을 시키다 'to assign work'.
E.g., 치킨을 시키다 'to order fried chicken'.

examples.trans: The team leader assigned this work to me.
Shall we order pizza for dinner?

meanings.note: Colloquial contraction of 그 아이 ('that child/kid'); used only for younger people or close peers.

examples.trans: Are you close with her?
He is late every day.

related.gloss: this kid / he or she (near speaker)
that kid / he or she (over there)

킬러.gloss: is a huge fan of, you see

meanings.en: is a huge fan of, you see
meanings.note: Used in spoken Korean dialogue (noun).

examples.text: 예진이가 먹고 싶은 거 위주로 시켰구먼, 걔가 산낙지 킬러거든.
examples.trans: Ye-jin clearly ordered all her own favorites—she is crazy about live octopus.
Here the word for 'is a huge fan of, you see' is key.

meanings.note: Negative copula used with nouns (often with -이/가)

examples.trans: It is not my fault.
Today is not Sunday, it's Monday.

meanings.note: Used in standard farewells 안녕히 계세요 and 안녕히 가세요.

examples.trans: Goodbye! (to someone staying)
Goodbye! (to someone leaving)

meanings.note: Honorific equivalent of 있다; used in 안녕히 계세요 ('goodbye' to someone staying).

examples.trans: Goodbye! (to someone staying)
Is the teacher inside right now?
